title: The Complete Malaysia Travel Guide
subtitle: Twin towers, tea-covered highlands and island coastline, split across a peninsula and a corner of Borneo
summary: How to plan a Malaysia trip: which region to choose, when to go around two separate monsoon seasons, what it costs, and a practical ten-day Peninsular Malaysia itinerary.

sections.title: How Malaysia divides
body: Malaysia splits into two physically separate halves across the South China Sea — a first trip realistically covers one.

**Peninsular Malaysia's west coast.** [[kuala-lumpur|Kuala Lumpur]], [[penang|Penang]], [[malacca|Malacca]], [[langkawi|Langkawi]], [[cameron-highlands|the Cameron Highlands]] and [[ipoh|Ipoh]] — cities, hill stations and heritage towns connected by good roads and rail.

**Peninsular Malaysia's east coast.** [[perhentian-islands|the Perhentian Islands]] and [[taman-negara|Taman Negara]] — beaches, diving and ancient rainforest, on a very different monsoon calendar from the west coast.
**East Malaysia (Borneo).** [[kota-kinabalu|Kota Kinabalu]] and [[kuching|Kuching]] — Sabah and Sarawak, reached only by air, with Mount Kinabalu, orangutans and longhouse culture.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors pick the Peninsula's west coast — it works as a complete trip on its own and doesn't require a single domestic flight beyond arrival.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[kuala-lumpur|Kuala Lumpur]], [[penang|Penang]] and [[malacca|Malacca]], the classic Peninsular introduction.

list.title: If you want cooler weather and green scenery
list.text: [[cameron-highlands|The Cameron Highlands]], a genuine change of pace from the tropical lowlands.

list.title: If you want beach resorts with easy access
list.text: [[langkawi|Langkawi]], reachable by a short flight or ferry with no monsoon complications on the west coast.

list.title: If you want serious diving and a backpacker pace
list.text: [[perhentian-islands|The Perhentian Islands]], best fit into a March–October trip.

list.title: If you want rainforest and wildlife over beaches
list.text: [[taman-negara|Taman Negara]], among the world's oldest rainforests.

list.title: If you want a dedicated Borneo trip
list.text: [[kota-kinabalu|Kota Kinabalu]] and [[kuching|Kuching]], best planned as their own separate itinerary.

sections.title: Getting around: flights, trains and one common mistake
body: The Peninsula's west coast is easy to cover by train and coach; Borneo and the east coast islands need their own flights.
**Don't try to combine the Peninsula and Borneo in one short trip.** [[kota-kinabalu|Kota Kinabalu]] and [[kuching|Kuching]] both need a dedicated domestic flight and add several days on their own.
**Use the KTM ETS train for the west coast corridor.** [[kuala-lumpur|Kuala Lumpur]], [[ipoh|Ipoh]] and [[penang|Penang]] are connected by frequent, comfortable high-speed rail.
**Check the east coast monsoon before booking.** [[perhentian-islands|The Perhentian Islands]] largely close from November to February — this catches first-time planners out more than anything else.
**Rent a car for the highlands.** [[cameron-highlands|The Cameron Highlands]] are far easier to explore at your own pace with your own vehicle.
sections.note: Book Sabah or Sarawak flights well ahead if adding Borneo — seats on the popular Kuala Lumpur routes fill up in peak holiday periods.

sections.title: When to go
body: Malaysia is hot and humid year-round, so 'the best time' really means picking a coast rather than a season.
**December to February** is the driest stretch for the west coast — Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Malacca, Langkawi and the highlands.
**March to October** is the main season for the east coast — the Perhentian Islands and Taman Negara's river access.
**November to February** brings the northeast monsoon to the east coast, closing most island resorts and complicating river trips inland.
sections.note: If a trip has to pick just one season, December to February works well for everywhere except the east coast islands and rainforest interior.

list.title: Five days: Kuala Lumpur and Malacca
list.text: A focused city-and-heritage-town introduction, flying into Kuala Lumpur.
list.tip: Malacca works well as a two-night side trip rather than a rushed day return.

list.title: Ten days: the classic Peninsular loop
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:malaysia|Malaysia country page]]: [[kuala-lumpur|Kuala Lumpur]], [[malacca|Malacca]], [[cameron-highlands|the Cameron Highlands]], [[ipoh|Ipoh]], [[penang|Penang]] and [[langkawi|Langkawi]]. A complete first look at the west coast.
list.tip: Book Langkawi's cable car for early morning — cloud cover often rolls in by early afternoon.

list.title: A week focused on the east coast
list.text: [[perhentian-islands|The Perhentian Islands]] and [[taman-negara|Taman Negara]], best combined between March and October.
list.tip: Fly into Kota Bharu or Kuala Terengganu rather than routing everything through Kuala Lumpur.

list.title: A dedicated Borneo add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[kota-kinabalu|Kota Kinabalu]] and [[kuching|Kuching]], the parts of Malaysia most first-time visitors never see.
list.tip: Book Mount Kinabalu climb permits months ahead — daily numbers are capped and popular dates sell out.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Malaysia?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers Peninsular Malaysia's west coast properly, such as the itinerary in this guide. Borneo is best treated as a separate trip.

faq.q: Should I combine Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo in one trip?
faq.a: It's possible with three weeks or more, but most visitors get better value focusing on one region and returning for the other.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Malaysia?
faq.a: Not for the main west coast cities, which are well connected by train and coach, but a car helps for exploring the Cameron Highlands.

faq.q: When should I avoid the Perhentian Islands?
faq.a: November through February, when the northeast monsoon brings rough seas and most island resorts close for the season.
